parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Children read short, decodable sentences that practise the sound /sh/ (spelled sh). Every other word uses only letter-sounds they have already learned, so they can sound the whole sentence out. Reading the page three times builds reading speed and confidence.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 15 minutes)
text: 1. Say the sound /sh/ together. Tell children sh is two letters that make one sound — like a quiet 'shhh'.
2. Read the first sentence together. Point under each word as you read.
3. Have children underline the sh in each sentence first, then read each sentence on their own.
4. Children read the whole page three times and colour one face each time.

parts.title: Answer key (the sh words)
text: Your turn: any real word with sh, e.g. shed, shut, wish, cash, brush.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: B2.3 — identify, read, and spell most common grapheme-phoneme correspondences of consonants and vowels, with automaticity.
In plain terms: children quickly read and spell the everyday letter-sounds — here, the digraph sh.

parts.title: If children get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: reading s and h as two sounds. Cover the rest of the word and say 'sh' first.
Make it easier: read only the first three sentences; you read, the child echoes.
Make it harder: ask the child to write their own sh sentence on the back.
You'll know it worked when: the child reads the page smoothly the third time and spots sh on sight.
